newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Mahathir's son wants to be judged as professional.
newsitem.headline: Mahathir's son wants to be judged as professional.

text.p: Running a company and being the son of the prime minister may be some people's idea of having it made, but Mokhzani Mahathir expects his work to be judged like that of any other professional.
"I don't expect my father's name to protect me if I mess up," said the 35-year-old son of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and chief executive of Tongkah Holdings Bhd.

Mokhzani Mahathir, whose expanding company may soon seek public listing for more of its units, says he has heard his share of criticisms about the perceived privileges afforded to children of the well-connected.
"It doesn't work that way. We go there as professionals and we expect to be treated as professionals," he told Reuters in a rare interview.

In a region where an especially high premium is placed on political connections and birthrights, the 70-year-old prime minister has made it clear that he does not want his children to be perceived as getting handouts in business.

Hence, Mokhzani and Mahathir's oldest son, Mirzan, who runs the transportation firm Konsortium Perkapalan Bhd, have distanced themselves from businesses involving government licensing, such as telecommunications.
But even where there are opportunities to bid for projects, Mokhzani says there can still be some second-guessing.
"If we go into a bidding process, we do a proposal. It's not going to be a shoddy thing, where we put out a bad proposal and expect...(an endorsement) just because of who we are," he said.

Mokhzani, a U.S.-educated petroleum engineer, joined Tongkah in 1990, and transformed the sleepy plantations company into a diversified conglomerate focusing on financial and medical services, and manufacturing.

He controls about 13 percent of the company, and in the past several years has been snapping up interests in Internet services, laundry, stockbroking and hospital firms. Tongkah reported operating profit of 25 million ringgit ($9.92 million) and 528.1 million turnover in the year ended June 30, 1996.
The soft-spoken Mokhzani says managing people is a priority. He cites his years as an offshore rig engineer with an oil company as his education in working with people.

"I was offshore on a seven-day on, seven-day off shift," he said. "When you work offshore, you're confined to a 50,000, 60,000 square feet (of platform). Absolutely no privacy out in the middle of the sea. You are on your toes all the time.
"It teaches you a lot about people management. The people who work on the oil patch are very tough people," he said.

Mokhzani said his days in that no-nonsense industry have shaped his view of work. He seems accessible, coming out personally to greet guests with sleeves rolled up. "There's a very short and clear route to me," he said.
